Some information about what ASC-T is.
It's a dynamically ASC-A-S-C-T dynamically adjust signal timings in real-time,
based on current traffic conditions.
These systems operate through three key steps.
Detection, analysis, and signal adjustment.
There are some benefits, reduced travel times, improved progression along a corridor,
decreased fuel consumption and vehicle emissions, and more reliable travel conditions.
Next slide, please.
ASC-T is, most effective for corridors where traffic demand varies significantly throughout the day,
such as commercial areas with many driveway or event venues.
It can respond to unexpected conditions such as incidents, construction, weather events,
or special events.
It is not appropriate or necessary for every location.
And it is used in corridors with highly consistent traffic patterns,
often achieved similar performance using well-designed time of day signal timing plans at a lower cost.
So they're not appropriate or necessary everywhere.
Next slide, please.
There are three types.
The first type is a traffic response of the system.
It is the most basic system.
Selects from a library or pre-developed timing plans based on current conditions.
The second type is adaptive, and it is a more advanced system that continuously monitors traffic
conditions and calculates signal timing adjustments in real-time.
And third is a predictive system.
It is the most advanced system and incorporates predictive analytics and artificial intelligence techniques to anticipate.
Future traffic conditions based on real-time and historical data then makes proactive timing adjustments.
Next slide, please.
A jurisdictional scan of Canadian experiences with ASCT was completed.
Victoria Vancouver and Edmonton do not use ASCT.
Coquillum uses a predictive system on one commercial corridor,
and Calgary uses an adaptive system on 11 intersections.
Next slide, please.
When it can go off, do not use ASCT.
Toronto uses an adaptive system at 220 intersections.
Ottawa uses an adaptive system on targeted corridors.
Montreal uses an adaptive system at 100 intersections.
And Quebec City is currently piloting an adaptive system.
Next slide, please.
To help with the discussion and assessment, we develop three options.
Number one, do not implement ASCT.
Under this option, the existing link project
designed with proceed without modification.
Conventional Accordinated Signal timing and TSP traffic signal priority
would be used to support corridor operations.
Number two, we could pilot on Circle Drive North between avenues C, north and Miller Avenue.
This option involves implementing ASCT at a location to evaluate system performance
to help determine the corridors where there is best return on investment.
This approach allows the city to test technology in a suitable environment
for rolling out to additional corridors.
Third, we could implement on Calls Drive and or First Avenue.
This option would incorporate ASCT into the Calls Drive link corridor
between Clarence Avenue and Preston Avenue and or the First Avenue link
between 20th Street and 25th Street.
This should require additional detection infrastructure and system integration.
